newsitem.title: INDIA: McDonnell Douglas seeks components from India.
newsitem.headline: McDonnell Douglas seeks components from India.

text.p: Leading U.S. aircraft manufacturer McDonnell Douglas said on Monday it planned to source sophisticated aircraft equipment from India for use in its MD-80 and MD-90 models.

Vice President and General Manager Donald Black, in charge of sales and marketing, told Reuters the firm was planning to award a contract valued at around $3 million initially to Tata Industries, part of India's largest business group.
"We're probably within 30 to 60 days of concluding a contract," said Donald Black, the firm's vice-president and general manager (sales and marketing). "They may be the winners."
The decision is part of McDonnell Douglas' thrust into the Indian aviation market, which saw passenger traffic grow at an estimated 14.2 percent last year, company officials said.

"We want to have a position in the booming Indian aviation market," said Mick Thackeray, the firm's regional vice-president (sales and marketing). "The deal will be worth millions of dollars to them over a period of years."

McDonnell Douglas is keenly competing with the U.S.'s Boeing and European consortium Airbus Industrie to sell about 20 aircraft to Air-India, India's national carrier, in a contract worth an estimated $2 billion.
It says its MD-11 is best suited to Air-India's requirements. Air-India has not yet made a decision.
Black said Tata might have to set up a new manufacturing facility to produce the equipment, to be used on McDonnell Douglas's MD-80 and MD-90 models.
"Within a short time, every MD-80 and MD-90 radome will probably be manufactured by the Tatas," Black told Reuters.

The radome is a nose cone that houses sophisticated radar equipment. It is made of materials called composites that can be penetrated by electromagnetic waves, John Graves, a McDonnell Douglas engineer, said.
Black said McDonnell Douglas wanted to manufacture radomes in India as part of the firm's overall strategy to outsource as many of its components as possible.
"It's essentially a transfer of production," he said. "We're making them a supplier."
"We're negotiating the unit price with the Tatas," Thackeray said. "They have the capability to manufacture the composites.
"We will provide the technology and ensure the product gets FAA (the U.S.'s Federal Aviation Authority) certification. That will enable the Tatas to bid for other orders."
Black said India's 14.2 percent airplane passenger growth last year led him to project sales of at least 40 McDonnell Douglas aircraft in the country by the year 2000.

Black, in India to demonstrate the MD-90 model, said some private domestic operators in India had expressed interest in buying McDonnell Douglas aircraft. He said the firm was in talks with Jet Airways and Tata Industries, among others.

Tatas' plan to set up a $400 million domestic airline in a joint venture with Singapore Airlines has been on hold for over a year, as the federal government hammers out a policy on the size of equity stake a foreign airline may hold.
